Where to put your Black Friday book $$
Time for the tradition of Black Friday overwhelm. If you’re a reader trying to navigate the day with calm, levity, and book smarts, you’ve come to the right place.
Here’s where to put your book money:
Shop local, as in your local bookstore. Some of us remember the kind of big box store Black Friday chaos that inspired Nana Kwame Adjei Brenyah’s titular short story in Friday Black.

Your local bookstore is far less likely to be inundated with crowds, and that’s why it’s all the more important to support them on a day dominated by big corporations. Just check that they’re open today.
Head over to Bookshop.org, the online bookseller that supports local bookstores.
From 11/27-11/30, they offer free Standard Shipping on all orders and 20% off their Best Books of the Year with code BESTBOOKS
On 11/28 only, you can get $15 Bookshop.org Tote Bags
ICYMI, Libro.fm has a Shop Small Sale running through November 30th. These sales also support local bookstores and are perfect for readers looking to put a book in their ear this holiday season.

The best book covers of November 2026
We all judge a book by its cover. There’s no shame in that–covers are the biggest marketing tool a book has.

But not all book covers are created equal. Some are better than others for reasons that range from being unique to giving a fresh twist to a design trend, or just because. Here are five November book covers that deserve a little shoutout for their designs. Design teams are credited where information is available.
Botany of Madness by Leon Engler, translated by Alexandra Roesch: The merging of birds and flowers is clever, evocative, and full of movement.
Clear Water by Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes (design team: Claire Sullivan and Laywan Kwan): Neon green is hot for font this year, and paired with the Silent Hill-style fog, the cover screams atmosphere.

Fieldwork as a Sex Object by Meena Kandasamy: This is the perfect embodiment of being trapped by the internet, and the cotton candy pink is jarring against the blue of the computer folders. There are several international covers for this one, but the U.S. version? Perfection.

The First House by Avni Doshi: The neon paired with a unique font choice would be enough, but what is that person doing atop that tower? It’s a novel about “rapture and rebirth,” and boy does this capture that!
Sweet Pea by Kit de Waal (design: Jonathan Bush): This one is all about the details of the flowers, the bright colors, and our gorgeous character at the center who begs the reader to open the story.
There were many good covers this month, and it’s always great when some of the best covers are for books that may otherwise go under the radar. – KJ
Nonfiction books about books and reading
It is a truth universally acknowledged that readers love books about books. Lucky for us, there’s no shortage of titles on the subject!
Here are three recent nonfiction releases about books and reading, from a philosophical collection of essays to a guide to determining your reading type.

Every Day I Read: 53 Ways to Get Closer to Books by Hwang Bo-Reum, translated by Shanna Tan – A delightful collection of essays celebrating books, reading, and language from the author of the bestselling slice-of-life novel, Welcome to the Hyunam-dong Bookshop
Read Your Color by Steven J. Reese* – Fall (or fall back) in love with reading using a six-type system to help you choose books based not on what you’ve read, but why you read.

Receipts from the Bookshop: A Bookseller’s Year in an English Seaside Town by Katie Clapham – A fun, dishy chronicle of a year in the life of a bookseller, from the owner of a family-owned bookstore in a seaside English town behind the Receipt from the Bookshop Substack
Zeba Shahnaz is the author of The Peacock Throne, out now from Delacorte Press. Below, she recommends three more fantasy novels inspired by South Asia.

It’s been so amazing for me, as an American author of Pakistani descent, to see the different ways that authors of South Asian origin have been channeling their myriad inspirations to create new worlds, develop compelling characters, and tell stories that stay with you long after you’ve turned the last page.

And in my case, as well as those of the amazing books in this list, South Asia is more than the cherry on top of the sundae (or, to keep it on theme, the basil seeds on top of the falooda): It’s the whole dessert.
The Candle and the Flame by Nafiza Azad

This lyrical, stirring novel stars Fatima, one of the few human survivors of a massacre in the city of Noor who must save the city from a terrible conspiracy. Though it’s located on the Silk Road, Noor most closely resembles a diverse South Asian city, and it’s so beautifully realized that it makes you feel nostalgic even as you’re still getting to know it.
The Silver Kingdom by Radiya Hafiza

This new dual-POV South Asian romantasy is a book after my heart. Set in a world inspired by the Indian subcontinent after it was divided into two and then three independent countries, it takes the tropes you know and love—Chosen One prophecies, warring kingdoms, forbidden lovers—and applies them to a new postcolonial context that feels fresh and modern.
Monsters Born and Made by Tanvi Berwah

The righteous anger of this book’s main character, Koral, as she forces herself into the upper class’s chariot race (featuring the monstrous maristags), draws you through a world that might seem like no South Asian fantasy you’ve read before. But its critique of caste and class pushes the bounds of what a South Asian fantasy can look like, and does it with a ton of pulse-pounding action.
Romance trends to look for in 2027

As we head into a new year, you might be trying to get a handle on the ever-shifting sands of the Romancelandia landscape. Book Riot contributor and romance author Isabelle Popp has some predictions for trends we might see in mainstream romance in 2027, pulled from these sources:
Trends in the 2027 books available on review sites like NetGalley and Edelweiss
Patterns in self-published books and fanfiction
The vaguer forces of the zeitgeist—what’s trending more broadly in culture?
In continuing trends, expect to see more:
Dark and mafia romance as well as sports romances—thank you, Heated Rivalry
Genre twists in contemporary romance: think time loops/slips or paranormal elements
Westerns and seasonal offerings in travel romances, especially to Scotland
In SF/F romance: shifter and omegaverse romance, and more books that land somewhere between cozy and epic
Isekai, a subgenre commonly found in anime and manga about contemporary characters falling into fantastical worlds
A surge in romantic suspense, which has never gone away but is finding a new audience
Sentient object romances – there’s more where Wicker came from
More on each prediction + plus reading recs for each. —VD

When it comes to manga, I gravitate towards art that takes the expressive eyes and silhouettes typically found in the genre to interesting places, and the titles rounded up by Carolina Ciucci in this list of the most beautifully illustrated manga do just that.
From intricate lining and brushwork to realistic renderings, the following titles have some of the most gorgeous artwork.

Vagabond by Takehiko Inoue: The gorgeous, realistic illustration style in this long-running manga series really boosts the story of the real-life Japanese swordsman it follows. In the 1600s, Miyamoto Musashi barely survives the Battle of Sekigahara, only to be hunted. He’ll have to accept help from a monk and a childhood friend if he’s to survive.

Witch Hat Atelier by Kamome Shirahama: This Ghibli-esque, whimsical, and witchy series is super popular and just got an anime adaptation this year. Coco lives in a world where magic is reserved for a certain group of people, but one day she sees a traveling magician who changes everything she’s been told about being a witch.

The Guy She Was Interested In Wasn’t a Guy at All by Sumiko Arai: This sapphic, dynamically illustrated manga is widely known as “the Green Yuri.” High schooler Aya finds a kindred spirit in a mysterious employee dressed in all black at a CD shop. She develops a serious crush on him, not knowing that he’s actually Mitsuki, her female classmate.
Feast your eyes on these other beautifully illustrated manga. —EE
